questions.question: How do you do back-of-the-envelope estimation for system design? What numbers should you know?
questions.title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation: Capacity Planning for System Design
questions.direct_answer: Start with user count and daily active users (DAU). Convert to requests/sec (DAU × actions/user ÷ 86,400 × peak multiplier). Then estimate storage (rows × row size × retention), bandwidth (requests × payload size), and cache size (working set × object size). Know the key latency numbers: L1 cache 1ns, RAM 100ns, SSD 100μs, HDD 10ms, same-datacenter round trip 0.5ms, cross-continent 150ms.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to quickly size a system and determine whether a design is feasible before diving into architecture
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting lost in precise math instead of using order-of-magnitude estimates — the goal is feasibility, not accuracy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the estimation framework systematically: QPS → storage → bandwidth → cache → number of servers. Use powers of 2 fluently.

sections.title: Why Estimation Comes Before Architecture
sections.content:
Before drawing a single box on a whiteboard, you need to know the **order of magnitude** of the system you're designing. Is it handling 100 requests/second or 100,000? Does it store 1 GB or 1 PB? The answer determines whether you need a single PostgreSQL instance or a globally distributed cluster — and jumping to architecture without doing the math is the fastest way to over-engineer or under-design.

**Back-of-envelope estimation** isn't about precision — it's about feasibility. You're trying to determine whether your design is in the right ballpark, not calculate exact server counts. Getting within 2–5× of the real number is perfectly useful. Getting the order of magnitude wrong (thinking you need 10 servers when you need 1,000) leads to architectures that collapse under real traffic.

The skill has three parts: knowing the **reference numbers** (how fast is a network call? how much data fits on a disk?), having a **systematic framework** (QPS → storage → bandwidth → memory → servers), and being comfortable with **rough math** in your head (round everything, use powers of 2 and 10, verify order of magnitude).

sections.title: The Reference Numbers Every Engineer Should Know
sections.content:
These numbers don't need to be memorized exactly — knowing the order of magnitude is what matters. The table below covers the numbers that appear most frequently in system design interviews.

| Operation | Latency | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| L1 cache reference | ~1 ns | CPU-local, fastest possible |
| L2 cache reference | ~4 ns | Still on-chip |
| Main memory (RAM) | ~100 ns | ~100× slower than L1 |
| SSD random read | ~100 μs | ~1,000× slower than RAM |
| HDD random read | ~10 ms | ~100× slower than SSD |
| Same-datacenter round trip | ~0.5 ms | Network within one DC |
| Cross-region round trip | ~50–150 ms | US East ↔ EU West |

| Resource | Capacity |
|---|---|
| Single HDD | ~10 TB |
| Single SSD | ~1–4 TB |
| Single server RAM | ~256–768 GB |
| Network bandwidth (1 Gbps) | ~100 MB/s useful throughput |
| QPS per web server (Spring Boot) | ~5,000–20,000 (depends on work per request) |
| QPS per PostgreSQL | ~10,000–50,000 (depends on query complexity) |
| QPS per Redis | ~100,000+ (simple operations) |

The critical insight: **RAM is 1,000× faster than SSD, SSD is 100× faster than HDD, and network calls are 5,000× slower than RAM**. Every architectural decision that moves data closer to the CPU (caching) or avoids network calls (colocation) is working with these ratios.

sections.title: The Five-Step Estimation Framework
sections.content:
Apply this framework to any system design problem. The steps build on each other — each answer feeds the next calculation.

**Step 1 — QPS (Queries Per Second):**
Start with daily active users or daily volume, then derive per-second load. Always calculate both **average and peak**.

Example: "10 million tweets per day" → `10M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 115 tweets/sec average`. Peak is typically 3–10× average → **350–1,150 tweets/sec at peak**. Read-heavy system? Multiply by read-to-write ratio. 100:1 means **11,500–115,000 reads/sec**.

**Step 2 — Storage:**
Estimate per-object size × volume × retention period. A tweet: 280 chars text (~300 bytes) + metadata (~200 bytes) + media pointer (~100 bytes) ≈ **600 bytes**. 10M tweets/day × 600 bytes = **6 GB/day** → **2.2 TB/year** → **11 TB over 5 years** (fits on 2 HDDs).

**Step 3 — Bandwidth:**
QPS × average response size. If each tweet read returns 2 KB (text + metadata + user info): 115,000 reads/sec × 2 KB = **230 MB/sec** → needs ~2.5 Gbps outbound bandwidth.

**Step 4 — Memory (Cache sizing):**
Follow the 80/20 rule — 20% of data generates 80% of traffic. Cache the hot 20%: 10M tweets/day × 0.2 × 600 bytes × 7 days ≈ **8.4 GB** → fits easily in one Redis instance.

**Step 5 — Server count:**
Divide peak QPS by per-server capacity. If each Spring Boot server handles 10K req/sec: 115,000 reads/sec ÷ 10,000 = **12 servers** (round up, add buffer for failover → **15 servers**).

sections.title: The Trap: Precision Over Judgment
sections.content:
The biggest mistake in estimation isn't getting a number wrong — it's **spending too long on precise math instead of reaching a conclusion**. The interviewer wants to see that you can quickly determine feasibility, not that you can do long division.

**Round aggressively.** Use 100,000 instead of 86,400 seconds/day (the error is ~15%, which is irrelevant at this scale). Use powers of 2 for memory (1 KB = 1,000 bytes, not 1,024). Multiply before dividing to avoid small fractions.

**State your assumptions explicitly.** "I'm assuming 100:1 read-to-write ratio" or "I'll estimate average tweet size at 600 bytes including metadata." The interviewer cares about your reasoning process, not the exact numbers. Wrong assumptions with clear reasoning are better than correct numbers with no explanation.

**Verify the order of magnitude.** After calculating, ask: does this make sense? 12 servers for a Twitter-scale read path sounds reasonable. 1,200 servers would suggest something is wrong. 1 server would suggest you underestimated traffic. This gut check is the most valuable part of estimation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Daily active users × actions/day ÷ 86,400 = QPS baseline** — always start with this; then multiply by 2–3 for peak.
- **Storage math: QPS × message size × seconds/day × retention days** — state the assumptions explicitly.
- **1 million req/day ≈ 12 req/sec; 1 billion ≈ 12K req/sec** — memorize these anchor points.
- **Network throughput ceiling: 1–10 Gbps per commodity server** — at 10KB payload × 10K req/sec = 100MB/sec = 800Mbps; one server handles it.
- **The estimation IS the requirement gathering** — declaring "100ms read latency" and "99.9% availability" directly determines your architecture choices.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is the first thing interviewers evaluate in a system design session because it determines whether the architecture you propose is even in the right ballpark. The goal is not precision — it's establishing the order of magnitude that drives every subsequent component decision.

**The estimation framework:**
- Start with daily active users and their primary action: users × actions/day ÷ 86,400 seconds = average QPS; multiply by 2–3× for peak traffic
- Memorize the anchors: 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 req/sec; 1 billion ≈ 12K req/sec; these let you classify a system instantly as low/medium/high scale
- Storage: QPS × message size × seconds/day × retention days; state every assumption explicitly — interviewers score the reasoning process, not the precise number

**What the numbers tell you about architecture:**
- QPS determines server count: one application server handles ~1K–10K req/sec depending on work type; at 50K req/sec you need 10–50 servers and a real load balancer
- Storage growth determines whether you need time-series partitioning, tiered storage, or a columnar format for analytics
- Read-to-write ratio determines whether you need caching, read replicas, or both: a 100:1 read/write ratio is the classic caching candidate

**The two common errors:**
- Forgetting to multiply by peak traffic: average QPS is not the design point; size for 3× peak or you'll be paged on the first traffic spike
- Estimating storage without compression: Kafka messages compressed with LZ4 are 4–6× smaller than raw; PostgreSQL with TOAST handles large columns transparently

I recommend spending the first 5 minutes of any system design interview on this estimation — it signals engineering maturity and anchors every component decision to actual requirements.

questions.question: How do CDNs and edge caching reduce latency for global users? When should you use them?
questions.title: CDN and Edge Caching: Reducing Latency for Global Users
questions.direct_answer: A CDN caches content at edge servers in 200+ locations worldwide, reducing latency from 150ms (cross-continent) to 10-30ms (nearest edge). Use CDNs for static assets (images, CSS, JS), API responses with cache-friendly patterns, and video delivery. The key decisions are cache invalidation strategy (TTL vs purge), origin shield configuration, and cache key design for dynamic content.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of CDN architecture, cache invalidation trade-offs, and when CDN caching helps vs when it doesn't
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Caching personalized or authenticated responses at the edge without proper cache key design — serving one user's data to another
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss origin shield to prevent thundering herd on origin, edge computing (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge), and cache key normalization

sections.title: The Latency Problem That Server-Side Optimization Can't Fix
sections.content:
You can optimize your Spring Boot API to respond in 5ms, but if the user is in Mumbai and your server is in Virginia, the physics of light through fiber imposes a **150ms round-trip time** that no code change can eliminate. For a page load requiring 3 sequential API calls, that's 450ms of pure network latency before any rendering begins.

**CDNs (Content Delivery Networks)** solve this by caching your content at **edge servers** distributed globally — 200+ locations for major providers like CloudFront, Cloudflare, and Akamai. The first request from Mumbai hits your origin server in Virginia, but every subsequent request for the same resource is served from the CDN's Mumbai edge, with **sub-10ms latency**.

The non-obvious value isn't just latency — it's **origin protection**. A CDN serving cached responses means your origin servers handle dramatically fewer requests. During traffic spikes (product launches, viral content), the CDN absorbs the surge while your origin infrastructure stays stable. Without edge caching, every traffic spike hits your servers directly.

sections.title: What to Cache at the Edge and What to Keep at the Origin
sections.content:
The edge caching decision depends on two factors: **how often the content changes** and **whether it's personalized**.

**Cache aggressively at the edge:**
- Static assets (JS, CSS, images, fonts) — these change only on deploy. Set `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` with cache-busting filenames (`app.a3f2b1.js`). One year TTL, effectively forever.
- Public API responses that change infrequently (product catalog, country lists, exchange rates) — `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300` (5 minutes)
- HTML pages that are the same for every user (marketing pages, blog posts) — `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=3600` (`s-maxage` applies only to CDN, not browser)

**Never cache at the edge without careful design:**
- Authenticated responses — caching a response that includes user-specific data risks **serving User A's data to User B**. This is the most dangerous CDN mistake.
- Responses with `Set-Cookie` headers — CDNs may cache the cookie and replay it to other users
- Personalized content (recommendations, dashboards) — cache key must include the user identifier, which defeats the purpose of shared caching

The rule: if the `Authorization` header changes the response, don't use a shared CDN cache. Use a per-user cache (Redis) instead, or strip personalization into a separate client-side API call so the page shell can be cached while the personalized data loads dynamically.

sections.title: Cache Invalidation at the Edge: The Hard Problem
sections.content:
Edge caching turns cache invalidation from a single-server problem into a **globally distributed** one. When you update a product price, you need to invalidate the cached version across 200+ edge locations. Three approaches exist, each with trade-offs.

**TTL-based expiration** — set a reasonable TTL (5 minutes for product data, 1 hour for static pages) and accept that the content is stale until TTL expires. Simplest approach, works for content where brief staleness is acceptable. Most CDN traffic uses this model.

**Explicit purge** — call the CDN API to invalidate specific URLs or patterns. CloudFront processes purge requests in 1–5 minutes, Cloudflare in under 30 seconds. Useful for urgent updates (wrong pricing, legal takedowns). The caveat: purge APIs have rate limits (CloudFront allows 1,000 wildcard invalidations/month for free), and propagation isn't instant.

**Origin shield** solves the related problem of **cache stampede on the origin**. Without a shield, when a cached object expires at 200 edge locations, all 200 simultaneously request the origin. The origin shield is a single intermediate cache layer — all edge locations funnel through it, so the origin receives one request instead of 200. CloudFront, Cloudflare, and Fastly all support this.

The practical setup for a Spring Boot API: use `Cache-Control` headers in your HTTP responses to control CDN behavior. The application decides what's cacheable and for how long — the CDN obeys the headers. This keeps caching policy in your code, not in CDN configuration.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Origin-pull vs push** — CDNs pull content from origin on first miss and cache at the PoP; push pre-loads content before any request.
- **Cache-Control: max-age is the CDN TTL** — set appropriately per content type; static JS/CSS (immutable with hash filenames): 1 year.
- **CDNs can't cache POST or authenticated responses by default** — dynamic, user-specific content requires origin traversal.
- **Anycast routing routes users to the nearest PoP** — 200ms New York → Singapore becomes 5ms New York → New York CDN node.
- **Stale-while-revalidate removes the cold-start penalty** — serve the cached version immediately while fetching the fresh version in background.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
CDNs solve a problem that no amount of server-side optimization can fix: the speed of light. A user in Singapore querying an origin server in Virginia adds 150ms of irreducible network latency regardless of how fast the server responds. A CDN node in Singapore serves the same content with 5ms latency.

**How CDNs work:**
- A CDN has hundreds of Points of Presence globally; Anycast routing sends each user's request to the geographically nearest PoP
- On the first request from a PoP, the edge server fetches from origin and caches the response; subsequent requests from that region are served from the edge without touching origin
- Cache-Control headers drive the TTL: static assets with content-hash filenames get 1-year max-age; HTML gets 5 minutes; API responses that can be shared across users get 60 seconds; user-specific data doesn't cache at all

**What CDNs can and can't cache:**
- CDNs cache GET responses with public or shared cache-control headers; POST requests, authenticated responses, and user-specific content bypass the CDN to origin
- Dynamic content can still benefit from CDN edge logic (edge functions, A/B testing) but the response itself hits origin
- Cache invalidation is the hard problem: stale-while-revalidate serves the old version while fetching the fresh one in background; CDN purge APIs allow instant invalidation on content updates

**The operational subtlety:**
- A cache hit rate below 80–90% means your content is too dynamic or your TTLs are too short to justify CDN cost; measure cache-hit ratio per content type in your CDN dashboard

I recommend CDNs for any application with users distributed geographically, and always setting explicit Cache-Control headers per content type rather than relying on CDN default behavior.

questions.question: What is the circuit breaker pattern and how does it prevent cascade failures in distributed systems?
questions.title: Circuit Breaker Pattern: Preventing Cascade Failures in Distributed Systems
questions.direct_answer: A circuit breaker monitors calls to a downstream service and 'trips' (opens) when failures exceed a threshold, immediately returning a fallback response instead of waiting for timeouts. This prevents one failing service from consuming all caller threads and cascading failure across the system. After a cooldown, the breaker enters half-open state, allowing probe requests to test if the service has recovered.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of cascade failure mechanics and how circuit breakers protect the calling service, not the failing service
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting timeouts too high (30s default) so threads pile up before the breaker trips — the damage is done before protection kicks in
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the relationship between circuit breakers, bulkheads, retries, and timeouts as a layered resilience strategy; mention Resilience4j configuration

sections.title: The Cascade Failure That Circuit Breakers Prevent
sections.content:
When a downstream service starts failing, the natural instinct is to keep trying — retry the request, wait for the timeout, try again. But this instinct is exactly what causes **cascade failures**. Each request to the failing service occupies a thread for the full timeout duration (often 30 seconds by default). At 100 requests/second, that's 3,000 threads blocked within 30 seconds. Your thread pool is exhausted, your service can't handle any requests — including ones that don't depend on the failing service — and the failure propagates upstream.

A **circuit breaker** detects that a downstream service is unhealthy and **stops calling it** before your own service is damaged. Instead of waiting 30 seconds per request for a service that's clearly down, the circuit breaker returns an immediate failure or fallback response. Your threads stay free, your service stays responsive, and the failing dependency gets breathing room to recover.

The name comes from electrical circuit breakers — when current exceeds safe levels, the breaker trips and cuts the circuit. Same principle: when error rates exceed a threshold, stop the flow of requests.

sections.title: The Three States: How a Circuit Breaker Decides
sections.content:
A circuit breaker operates as a state machine with three states, and the transitions between them are what make it useful.

**Closed** (normal operation) — all requests pass through to the downstream service. The breaker monitors the failure rate in a sliding window. If failures exceed the threshold (e.g., 50% of the last 10 requests fail), the breaker **trips open**.

**Open** (protection mode) — all requests fail immediately without calling the downstream service. No threads are blocked, no network calls are made. The breaker returns either a pre-defined **fallback response** (cached data, default value, degraded functionality) or a fast error. After a configurable **wait duration** (e.g., 30 seconds), the breaker transitions to half-open.

**Half-open** (probe mode) — the breaker allows a **limited number of trial requests** through to test if the downstream service has recovered. If these succeed, the breaker **closes** (back to normal). If they fail, the breaker **opens** again and resets the wait timer.

The Resilience4j implementation makes this concrete — configuring the breaker sets the sliding window size, failure rate threshold, and wait duration. The sliding window can be count-based (last N requests) or time-based (last N seconds), each suited to different traffic patterns.

sections.title: Resilience4j Configuration: The Settings That Matter
sections.content:
Resilience4j is the standard circuit breaker library for Spring Boot (Hystrix is deprecated). The configuration requires understanding what each parameter actually controls — setting them wrong either triggers false positives or fails to protect.

A production-ready configuration specifies the sliding window, failure thresholds, and recovery behavior explicitly rather than relying on defaults.

```java
@Bean
public CircuitBreakerConfig paymentServiceBreakerConfig() {
    return CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
        .slidingWindowType(SlidingWindowType.COUNT_BASED)
        .slidingWindowSize(10)               // evaluate last 10 calls
        .failureRateThreshold(50)            // trip at 50% failure rate
        .waitDurationInOpenState(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
        .permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState(3)
        .slowCallDurationThreshold(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .slowCallRateThreshold(80)           // 80% slow calls also trips
        .build();
}
```

The **slow call threshold** is the setting most teams miss. A service that responds but takes 10 seconds per call is just as dangerous as one that returns errors — it still exhausts your thread pool. Setting `slowCallDurationThreshold` to 2 seconds and `slowCallRateThreshold` to 80% means the breaker trips when most calls are unacceptably slow, not just when they fail outright.

The **sliding window size** determines sensitivity. Too small (3 requests) and normal error variance trips the breaker. Too large (100 requests) and the breaker takes too long to detect real failures. 10–20 is the practical range for most services.

sections.title: Layered Resilience: Circuit Breakers Don't Work Alone
sections.content:
A circuit breaker is one component in a **layered resilience stack**. Each layer addresses a different failure mode, and configuring them correctly requires understanding how they interact.

**Timeouts** — set aggressively short, not the default 30 seconds. If a service normally responds in 100ms, a 2-second timeout catches degradation. Without short timeouts, threads accumulate waiting for slow responses before the circuit breaker even has enough data to trip.

**Retries** — retry transient failures (network blips, 503s) with exponential backoff. But retries must be **inside** the circuit breaker — if the breaker is open, retries should not execute. Retrying through an open breaker defeats its purpose.

**Bulkheads** — limit the number of concurrent calls to each downstream service. Even with circuit breakers, a burst of requests can temporarily exhaust threads before the breaker trips. A bulkhead (Resilience4j's `Bulkhead` or `ThreadPoolBulkhead`) caps concurrency so one failing dependency can't consume all your threads.

**The ordering matters:** timeout wraps the HTTP call, retry wraps the timeout, circuit breaker wraps the retry, bulkhead wraps everything. In Resilience4j annotations, the order of aspect execution is configurable but the default is: Bulkhead → CircuitBreaker → Retry → TimeLimiter. Getting this wrong — for example, retrying outside the circuit breaker — means retries continue even when the breaker should have stopped them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three-state machine: CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN** — CLOSED is normal; OPEN fails fast (no downstream attempt).
- **Failure threshold must exclude business errors** — HTTP 400 (bad request) and 422 (validation failure) are the caller's fault.
- **`slowCallDurationThreshold` catches degradation before hard failures** — a service responding in 5s instead of 200ms ties up threads just as badly as a.
- **Bulkhead isolation per dependency** — separate thread pools per downstream service.
- **Half-open probe count must be conservative** — too many probes during half-open overwhelm a recovering service and force it back to OPEN.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The circuit breaker prevents cascading failures in synchronous service chains. When a downstream service starts failing, the worst response is to keep sending requests — each waiting thread holds a connection and eventually exhausts the thread pool. The circuit breaker detects the failure pattern and fails fast, protecting the caller from spending resources on requests that will fail anyway.

**The three-state machine:**
- CLOSED is normal operation — all calls go through and failure metrics accumulate in a sliding window
- When failures exceed the threshold (typically 50% of the last 20 calls), the breaker opens — every call returns immediately with the fallback response without touching the downstream service
- After a wait duration (10–60 seconds), the breaker enters HALF_OPEN and allows a small number of probe calls through; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it

**Critical configuration decisions:**
- The failure filter: business validation errors (HTTP 400, 422) should NOT count toward the failure rate — only infrastructure failures (timeout, connection refused, HTTP 503) should trip the breaker; misconfiguring this causes the breaker to open on bad user input
- Slow call threshold: a service responding in 5 seconds ties up threads just as badly as a hard failure; set slowCallDurationThreshold to 2–3× your expected p99 latency to detect degradation before threads exhaust
- Probe count in HALF_OPEN must be conservative — overwhelming a recovering service forces it immediately back to OPEN

**Composing with bulkheads and retries:**
- Bulkheads (separate thread pools per dependency) prevent a failing inventory service from exhausting the pool that payments and shipping also use
- Retry should wrap around the circuit breaker — the breaker sees the aggregate outcome, not each individual retry attempt

I recommend Resilience4j with explicit `recordExceptions` configuration, alert on CLOSED→OPEN transitions as production incidents, and pair every circuit breaker with a bulkhead to isolate the impact of each downstream dependency.
